--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.minimum_cost_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute minimum cost flow from source to sink. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.minimum_cost_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute minimum cost flow from source to sink. title: >- [Graph.minimum_cost_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute minimum cost flow from source to sink. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute minimum cost flow from source to sink. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L81064-L81268){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.minimum_cost_flow( source, target, demand=None, capacity=None, cost=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum cost flow](../assets/graphs/minimum-cost-flow.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The maximum_flow network with a per-unit cost on each edge, labeled flow/capacity then cost. Sending a demand of 4 from S to T at the lowest cost fills S→A, then splits at A between the cheap detour A→B→T and the direct A→T; the costly S→B stays unused and faded. The card lists flow times cost per edge and the totals: flow 4, cost 14." width="100%"} Every edge has a *capacity* (the most flow it can carry) and a *cost* per unit of flow. This method routes flow from `source` to `target` so that the total cost is as small as possible. It can either push a fixed amount of flow (`demand=`) or push as much flow as the network can carry and, among all maximum flows, return the cheapest one. Where `maximum_flow()` only asks "how much can get through?", min cost flow also asks "what is the cheapest way to send it?". That makes it a natural fit for: - transportation and logistics problems (shipping goods from suppliers to customers) - assignment problems (matching workers to jobs at minimum total cost) - routing traffic or data where links have both a bandwidth limit and a price - any planning problem that can be phrased as "move X units through a network cheaply" The algorithm is Successive Shortest Path: it repeatedly finds the cheapest augmenting path in the residual network (using Bellman-Ford, so negative per-unit costs are allowed) and pushes as much flow along it as the bottleneck capacity permits. The graph must be directed. Self-loops are ignored. Every edge is routed on its own, so parallel edges between the same pair of nodes each keep their own capacity and cost (the cheaper one fills first) and `flow_dict` reports each one's flow separately. Edges in opposite directions between two nodes are also independent of each other. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node where flow originates, given as an integer node ID or a string label. The node must already exist in the graph. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node where flow is absorbed, given as an integer node ID or a string label. Must exist in the graph and be different from `source=`. [demand]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The exact amount of flow to send from `source=` to `target=`. If `None` (the default), the method sends the maximum possible flow and returns the cheapest way of doing so. If a number is given, exactly that much flow is sent at minimum cost; a `ValueError` is raised if the network cannot carry that much. Must be non-negative. [capacity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding each edge's capacity. If `None` (the default), each edge's capacity is taken from its `"capacity"` attribute if present, otherwise from the edge weight on a weighted graph, otherwise `1.0`. If a name is given, every edge must hold a numeric value for it (`"weight"` also accepts the edge weight), otherwise a `ValueError` is raised. [cost]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding the cost per unit of flow. If a name is given, every edge must hold a numeric value for it, otherwise a `ValueError` is raised. If `None` (the default), each edge's `"cost"` attribute is used, and edges lacking it (or holding a non-numeric value) get a per-unit cost of `1.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[float, float, dict[int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A tuple containing: (1) `total_flow`, the total amount of flow sent; (2) `total_cost`, the sum over all edges of flow times per-unit cost; and (3) `flow_dict`, a dictionary mapping edge IDs to the flow they carry. Only edges with positive flow appear in `flow_dict`. If no path exists and `demand=` is `None`, the result is `(0.0, 0.0, {})`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected, `source=` or `target=` doesn't exist, they're the same node, `demand=` is negative, `demand=` cannot be satisfied, or a cycle whose per-unit costs sum to a negative number is reachable from `source=` (the cheapest flow is then undefined), or an edge lacks the attribute named by `capacity=` or `cost=`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Uses the Successive Shortest Path algorithm with Bellman-Ford relaxation, so negative per-unit costs are permitted alongside the usual non-negative case (a reachable negative-cost cycle raises `ValueError`, since a cheapest path is then undefined). The algorithm runs in $O(V \cdot E \cdot F)$ time in the worst case, where $F$ is the number of augmenting steps. Because it always routes along the *cheapest* residual path from source to sink, the final flow is optimal in total cost for the amount sent. The graph must be directed (call `.to_directed()` first for undirected inputs), and self-loops contribute nothing. Leaving `demand=` at `None` sends the maximum possible flow at minimum cost; setting it to a specific value clamps the total and raises `ValueError` if that demand cannot be met by any admissible flow. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~maximum_flow`) : The largest flow, regardless of cost. [](`~minimum_cut`) : The cut that limits the largest flow. ## Examples {.doc-examples} With two possible paths from `S` to `T`, the flow fills the cheaper route through `A` (per-unit cost 2) before the dearer one through `B` (per-unit cost 3). The edge weights act as capacities, since no `"capacity"` attribute is present: ::: {#69b1cf56 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("S", "A", 10.0, {"cost": 1.0}), ("S", "B", 10.0, {"cost": 2.0}), ("A", "T", 10.0, {"cost": 1.0}), ("B", "T", 10.0, {"cost": 1.0}), ], directed=True, ) total_flow, total_cost, flow_dict = graph.minimum_cost_flow("S", "T") total_flow, total_cost ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (20.0, 50.0) ``` ::: ::: The third element maps edge IDs to flow. Every edge carries its full capacity of 10: ::: {#ebad50b7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.set_edge_attrs("flow", flow_dict).get_edge_df(labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

Fifteen units fill the route through `A` and send the rest through `B`: ::: {#1c3bd36a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.minimum_cost_flow("S", "T", demand=15.0)[:2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (15.0, 35.0) ``` ::: ::: Capacity and cost can come from any attributes. Here the cheap two-hop route `A -> B -> C` (cost 8 per unit) fills up to its bottleneck of 50 before the pricier direct edge (cost 10) carries the remaining 30: ::: {#1b6a555c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("A", "B", {"bandwidth": 100, "price": 5}), ("B", "C", {"bandwidth": 50, "price": 3}), ("A", "C", {"bandwidth": 30, "price": 10}), ], directed=True, ) graph.minimum_cost_flow("A", "C", capacity="bandwidth", cost="price")[:2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (80.0, 700.0) ``` ::: ::: A transportation problem fits the same mold: a super-source feeds the warehouses, with each edge's capacity its supply, and the stores drain into a super-sink, with each edge's capacity its demand. Meeting the stores' 90 units costs 410, with each store supplied from its nearer warehouse: ::: {#034442d7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("Source", "W1", 50.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ("Source", "W2", 60.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ("W1", "S1", 100.0, {"cost": 8.0}), ("W1", "S2", 100.0, {"cost": 5.0}), ("W2", "S1", 100.0, {"cost": 4.0}), ("W2", "S2", 100.0, {"cost": 7.0}), ("S1", "Sink", 40.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ("S2", "Sink", 50.0, {"cost": 0.0}), ], directed=True, ) flow, cost, assignment = graph.minimum_cost_flow( "Source", "Sink", demand=90.0 ) cost ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 410.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Water at the lowest cost `pipeline()` is a made-up city's water supply, with each pipe's `capacity` in megaliters a day and a running `cost` per megaliter, both of which `minimum_cost_flow()` reads without being told. The full 45 ML a day cost 285, but 30 ML cost only 170, since the smaller amount can leave the Hill Pump, the dearest pipe, idle: ::: {#6f36e67a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pipeline = ec.pipeline() _, full_cost, _ = pipeline.minimum_cost_flow("Reservoir", "City") sent, cost, flow = pipeline.minimum_cost_flow( "Reservoir", "City", demand=30 ) full_cost, cost ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (285.0, 170.0) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#e3b94b2f .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pipeline.set_edge_attrs("flow", flow) pipeline.plot( layout="pos", label_by="label", edge_width_by="flow", edge_label_by="cost", width=700, height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
